html:
The Panama scandals were a French financial and political scandal in 1892 and 1893 that followed the collapse of the company building the first Panama Canal. The company, led by Ferdinand de Lesseps, failed in 1889 after disease, landslides and debts. Hundreds of thousands of small French investors lost their savings.

In 1892 the newspaper La Libre Parole, edited by the antisemite Edouard Drumont, charged that the company had paid journalists and members of parliament to speak well of it and to pass a lottery bond issue. Names of deputies and ministers came out. Two of the middlemen, Jacques de Reinach and Cornelius Herz, were Jewish, and Drumont turned the case into an attack on Jews and on the republic.

In 1893 Lesseps, his son Charles and the engineer Gustave Eiffel were convicted of fraud, though the verdicts were soon overturned on a technicality. Only one minister was convicted. Many politicians survived, but the affair shook faith in the Third Republic and fed the hatred that surfaced again in the Dreyfus affair in 1894. The canal was later taken up by the United States.
